passage:
Last winter I forgot to pick Trisha up from the railway station. Her train came in at 11:40 p.m.; she waited forty minutes on a cold platform, her phone battery dying, before taking an auto home alone. I had fallen asleep in front of a match.
My first instinct was to explain: long week, she should have called twice. I'd done that before, and I'd seen how excuses made her feel like the problem was hers. So the next morning I said it plainly: "I forgot you. You were alone at midnight on a platform because of me. I'm sorry." No "but". Then I asked, "What would help, now and next time?" She said she needed to know I'd take her safety seriously. So now her train times go into my phone with two alarms, and I text her when I leave home. Later she told me it was the first apology from me that felt finished. I'm Ojas, and I'm still learning.

qa.q: How long did Trisha wait on the platform?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Ojas resist the first instinct to explain?
qa.a: Ojas remembered that excuses had made Trisha feel the problem was hers, and wanted her to feel the harm was truly understood.

qa.q: Which step made the apology 'feel finished' to Trisha?
qa.a: Asking what would help and then changing behaviour, with train-time alarms and a text when leaving, so the words were followed by something she could rely on.

qa.q: What was that night like for Trisha?
qa.a: Cold, frightening and lonely, waiting at midnight with a dying phone before taking an auto home alone.

grounding: An adult names exactly what went wrong, apologises without excuses, asks what would help and changes behaviour, so the repair can be felt.

passage:
Team lead's note, Friday
On Monday, Lavanya lost her temper with our intern, Meghna, in the open office and called her work "useless" in front of everyone. Meghna left early, in tears.
I planned to step in, but Lavanya got there first. On Tuesday morning she asked Meghna for a private word, and I was present at Meghna's request. Lavanya said, "On Monday I called your work useless in front of the team. That was wrong and unfair. I'm sorry." She didn't mention her own stress or deadline. Then she asked, "What would help you now?" Meghna asked for clearer instructions in writing.
Since then Lavanya has sent written briefs every morning and gives any feedback privately. Meghna told me today that she feels safe asking questions again.
Charu

qa.q: What did Lavanya call Meghna's work on Monday?
qa.a: "Useless", in front of everyone.

qa.q: Why might Lavanya have left her own stress and deadline out of the apology?
qa.a: She seemed to understand that mentioning them would sound like an excuse and pull attention away from Meghna's hurt.

qa.q: What made Lavanya's repair work beyond the words?
qa.a: She asked what would help, then sent written briefs every morning and gave feedback privately, so Meghna could feel the change.

qa.q: What would have changed for Meghna if Lavanya had only said, 'Sorry, I was stressed'?
qa.a: Meghna might have felt the blame was still partly hers, and without written briefs she might have stayed afraid to ask questions.

grounding: A team lead records how a colleague who publicly insulted an intern named it, apologised without excuses, asked what would help and changed her behaviour.

passage:
Tuesday night
Today I finally did it properly. Two weeks ago I dropped Pranav's camera at the beach and cracked the lens. I put it back in his cupboard and said nothing for a week. When he found it, I mumbled something about sand getting in. Awful.
Tonight I knocked on his door. I said, "I broke your camera at the beach, and then I hid it and blamed the sand. Both were wrong. I'm sorry." I didn't say "but". I asked what would help. He said the lens mattered less than the hiding. He wanted to be able to trust me with his things again.
So I've ordered a replacement lens from my savings, and from now on I ask before borrowing and tell him the same day if anything goes wrong.
He shrugged and said, "Okay. Thanks for saying the whole thing." That felt better than any excuse ever has.
Ishita

qa.q: Where did Ishita drop Pranav's camera?
qa.a: At the beach.

qa.q: What was Pranav most upset about, and why?
qa.a: The hiding, because it damaged his trust in lending things far more than the cracked lens did.

qa.q: Which parts of Ishita's apology made it a real repair?
qa.a: Naming both the breaking and the hiding without excuses, asking what would help, replacing the lens and changing how borrowing works. 🙏

qa.q: What would have changed if Ishita had stuck to the sand story?
qa.a: Pranav's trust would probably have kept wearing away, since he would sense the truth was being hidden.

grounding: An adult replaces a hidden, excuse-filled cover-up with a full apology, asks what would help and changes how they borrow, so the repair is felt.

passage:
"Sarita, can you water the tulsi and fold the towels before dinner?"
"Yes, Mummy! Of course!"
An hour later: "Sarita, the towels?"
"Oh! I forgot. Sorry! I'll do it right now!"
Half an hour later Himani-didi came in. "Mummy, the towels are still in the basket. And the tulsi's dry again."
"Sarita?"
"I totally forgot! My brain is so bad."
"That's the fifth time this week, beta."
Sarita looked at her toes. Didi sat down next to her. "You know what I think? I think you hate folding towels."
"...I do hate folding towels. They're so boring. And Didi only has to do the dishes."
"Then say that," Mummy said. "We can talk about swapping. But saying yes and then forgetting isn't fair on anyone."

qa.q: What two jobs did Mummy ask Sarita to do?
qa.a: Water the tulsi and fold the towels.

qa.q: Why did Sarita keep saying yes and then forgetting?
qa.a: Sarita didn't want the boring job and felt it was unfair next to Didi's, but found it hard to say no directly, so the resistance came out as forgetting.

qa.q: Which choice in the conversation opened a better way forward?
qa.a: Didi naming the likely feeling, then Mummy inviting Sarita to say it and offering to talk about swapping. 🙂

qa.q: How might Himani-didi feel about the dry tulsi and the unfolded towels?
qa.a: Probably irritated at noticing the undone jobs again, and perhaps a little defensive when the dishes were brought up.

grounding: A child cheerfully agrees to a chore and keeps forgetting, until Mummy and Didi help Sarita say directly what the problem is.

passage:
Last month Rafiq Chacha from next door asked if I'd feed his parrots every evening while his leg was in plaster. I said, "Yes, yes, definitely!" And then, three evenings out of five, I "forgot". Mummy had to go instead, and she looked at me funny at dinner.
The truth, which I didn't even tell myself then, was that the parrots scare me. They screech and bite the bars when you open the cage. But Chacha is so kind, always giving me toffees, that saying no felt rude.
Last week Mummy asked why I kept agreeing. I cried a bit and told her. Then I told Chacha. He laughed and said, "Arre, just say so!" Now I water his plants instead. I'm Jahnavi, and plants don't bite.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Friday
For three weeks Shreya has been on the rota to wipe the board and water the class plants. Each morning she agrees brightly, "Yes, Nazia Ma'am!", and each afternoon the board is still full and the plants are dry. When I remind her, she says, "Oh no, I totally forgot!" with a big smile.

qa.q: Why might Shreya say 'I totally forgot!' with a big smile?

qa.q: What would change for Shreya now that Nazia Ma'am has said 'I won't be cross'?
qa.a: She may feel safe to say no openly next time, so she won't need to 'forget' to show she doesn't want a job.

grounding: A teacher notices a girl who agrees brightly to class jobs and then forgets them, and makes it safe for her to say no directly.

passage:
When Papa made the rule that my phone stays in the kitchen after ten, I didn't argue. I said "fine". Then I did everything he asked, just slowly. Emptying the dishwasher took forty minutes. I answered every question with "hmm" or "okay". When my brother Sumit asked if I wanted to play carrom, I said "no" and went back to my room to stare at the ceiling.
I thought I was being really mature, not shouting. Looking back, I was shouting, just quietly. Everyone could feel it.
On Sunday Papa sat on my bed and said, "You're allowed to be angry about the rule. I'd rather hear it than feel it." So I told him: my friends talk at night and I feel left out. We didn't scrap the rule, but we moved it to half past ten on weekends. I'm Mridul, fifteen, and I'm trying to use my words now.

qa.q: How long did Mridul take to empty the dishwasher?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did the slow chores and 'hmm' answers feel 'mature' to Mridul at the time?
qa.a: Not shouting felt grown-up, but Mridul was still angry about the rule, and the anger came out as quiet sulking.

qa.q: What choice of Papa's opened things up?
qa.a: Sitting on the bed and saying Mridul was allowed to be angry and he'd rather hear it, which led to a real talk and a weekend compromise.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt when Mridul refused to play carrom?
qa.a: Rejected and confused, caught in a mood that wasn't really about him.

grounding: A teenager who resents a new phone rule obeys with slow chores, scowls and one-word answers until a parent invites the anger out loud.

passage:
House-mother's note, Hostel B, Thursday
Since we brought in lights out at 10 p.m. for Class 11, Shalini has complied, in her own way. She switches off her lamp at 9:59 with a loud click. She takes twenty minutes to fold her uniform, scowling. When I say good morning, she says "morning" without looking up. Her roommate says she hasn't laughed all week.
I don't think Shalini is being defiant exactly. I think she's angry and doesn't see a safe way to say so. She is usually open and chatty.
Today I asked her to help me carry the laundry, and on the way I said, "I know you're not happy about lights out. Tell me what bothers you. I'd rather hear it than guess." She was quiet, then said she studies best late. We agreed she can use the common room till 10:30 twice a week before exams.
Kavitha, House-mother

qa.q: At what time does Shalini switch off her lamp?
qa.a: At 9:59, with a loud click.

qa.q: What does the loud click at 9:59 suggest Shalini is feeling?
qa.a: She is angry about the rule and shows it by obeying to the letter, since she doesn't see a safe way to say it directly.

qa.q: What choice of Kavitha's helped Shalini speak up?
qa.a: Inviting the complaint privately while they carried laundry, saying she'd rather hear it than guess, which made direct disagreement safe.

qa.q: How might Shalini's roommate experience this week?
qa.a: Probably tense and a bit gloomy, noticing Shalini hasn't laughed and unsure what's wrong.

grounding: A hostel house-mother notices a teenager obeying a new rule with scowls, slowness and monosyllables, and invites her to say her anger directly.

passage:
Saturday
Ma says I have to go to every single function of Seema Masi's daughter's wedding. All four days. Including the one on the night of my friend's birthday sleepover. I said "okay". I didn't say anything else all day.
I got ready for the haldi so slowly that Ma had to knock three times. I wore the orange suit she picked, but I scowled in every photo. When Masi asked if I was excited, I said "yes" like a robot. I ate one puri. I sat in the corner and answered my cousins with "hmm".
Here's the thing: I'm not actually mad at Masi. I'm mad at Ma for deciding without asking me. But if I say that, it'll turn into a big fight. So I'm being "obedient". Very, very slowly.
Maybe tomorrow I'll just tell Ma. Maybe.
Leela

qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Who is Leela really angry with, and why doesn't Leela say so?
qa.a: With Ma, for deciding without asking; Leela fears saying it will start a big fight, so the anger comes out as slow, silent obedience. 😠

qa.q: What could Leela try tomorrow instead of the slow scowl?
qa.a: Tell Ma calmly that deciding without asking hurt, and ask whether there's any room to talk about the birthday night.

qa.q: How might Seema Masi feel when Leela says 'yes' like a robot?
qa.a: Maybe hurt or confused, thinking Leela doesn't care about the wedding, when the anger isn't about Masi at all.

grounding: A teenager who resents being made to attend every wedding function complies with scowls, slowness and one-word answers.

passage: Preeti, you're moving into the hostel next week, so let your Vijay Mama tell you about his first flat in Pune. I shared it with a boy called Mohan. One morning I found a note on the fridge: "Wow, you washed a plate! Should we call the newspapers?" Then another: "Thank you SO much for leaving your socks on the sofa. Very decorative." It was exam week, the water in their building came for only two hours a day, and Karthik had a thermodynamics paper at nine. At 6 a.m. he found a sticky note on the kettle in Sabina's handwriting: "Thanks SO much for washing your mug. For once. Truly a miracle." Another was stuck to the bucket: "Love how the water fills itself."

She blinked, then sighed. "I've been filling the buckets alone every morning. I'm exhausted too."
They split the mornings: he would take Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.

passage:
Gargi came back from the library to find a note on her pillow in their PG room in Mukherjee Nagar: "Thanks for the lovely music at 1 a.m.! I didn't need sleep anyway 🙂" The next day there was one on the mirror: "So kind of you to leave your hair in the sink. A gift!"
Gargi stared at the neat handwriting. Neelam, her roommate, was at her desk with headphones on, not looking up. Gargi's chest tightened. She wanted to rip the note off and say something clever and cutting. She had no idea how long Neelam had been angry.

Neelam went red. "The music at night, mostly. I have an early coaching class."
Gargi nodded. "Headphones after eleven. And I'll clear the sink. Deal?"

subtype: Yes in the meeting, delay afterwards [Observer]
passage:
At the NGO's Tuesday meeting, Chinmay laid out the new plan: the literacy survey would go digital, with tablets instead of paper forms. Eshaan, who ran the field team, nodded. "Sounds good."
Two weeks later the tablets were still in their boxes. The training date had slipped twice. The first batch of data arrived on paper. Each time Chinmay asked, Eshaan said, "Almost there," and smiled. Chinmay began to see a pattern: Eshaan had agreed to every part of the plan and delivered none of it. It wasn't laziness; Eshaan was the hardest worker in the building.
On Friday Chinmay closed the door of the small meeting room. "I don't think I ever asked what you really thought of the tablets. You can say no to my ideas here. What's wrong with the plan?"
Eshaan let out a long breath. "Half the villages have no charging points."

qa.q: What was the new plan for the literacy survey?
qa.a: It would go digital, with tablets instead of paper forms.

qa.q: Why might Eshaan have said 'Sounds good' in the meeting despite doubts?
qa.a: Eshaan may not have felt safe disagreeing in front of others, so the objection came out as quiet delays instead.

qa.q: What choice did Chinmay make on Friday, and why did it work?
qa.a: Closing the door and openly inviting a no, admitting the question had never been asked, which let Eshaan name the real problem of charging points.

qa.q: What might the last two weeks have been like for Eshaan?
qa.a: Stressful and stuck, knowing the plan wouldn't work in the villages but not feeling able to say so.

grounding: A manager sees a hard-working team member agree to a plan and then miss every milestone, and creates a private space to say no.

passage:
Subject: The launch timeline, and a question I should have asked
Hi Leela,
In our planning meeting on the 3rd, you agreed to the new launch date, and I moved on quickly. Since then the design review has slipped, the copy deadline has passed, and your updates say "nearly done". You're one of the most reliable people on this team, so I've been wondering what's going on.
I think I may have missed something. Looking back, I announced the date more than I discussed it. If you disagreed, I didn't make it easy to say.
So I'm asking now, with no penalty: do you think the date is realistic? What would you change? A straight "no" is welcome. I'd rather hear it now than find out at the next missed milestone.
Can we talk tomorrow at 11, just the two of us?
Chetan

qa.q: When was the planning meeting where Leela agreed to the launch date?
qa.a: On the 3rd.

qa.q: Why does Chetan think Leela might have kept quiet in the meeting?
qa.a: Chetan realises the date was announced rather than discussed, so disagreeing may not have felt easy or safe.

qa.q: What makes Chetan's email a good way to invite honesty?
qa.a: It admits Chetan's own part, promises no penalty, asks direct questions and welcomes a straight 'no', then offers a private talk.

qa.q: How might Leela feel reading 'A straight no is welcome'?
qa.a: Probably relieved and a bit nervous, finally allowed to say the date isn't realistic without it looking like failure.

grounding: A manager emails a reliable team member who agreed to a date and then kept slipping, admitting the disagreement was never invited and making it safe to say no.

subtype: Yes in the meeting, delay afterwards [Observer]
passage:
You want to know my biggest early mistake as a manager? Siddharth. He'd sit in every sprint planning, nod, and say, "Yep, doable." Then the week would end and his tasks would be untouched. Not late by a day. Untouched. I thought he was lazy, honestly. I nearly wrote him up.
Then a colleague said, "Manoj, have you ever seen anyone say no in your meetings?" I thought about it. Nobody had. I'd built a room where "yes" was the only safe word.
So I started ending planning with, "Okay, what here do you think is a bad idea?" and then waiting, awkwardly long. The third time, Siddharth said, "The API migration. It's going to break the billing system." He was right. We rescheduled it. His tasks started getting done.

qa.q: What did Siddharth say about the API migration?
qa.a: "It's going to break the billing system."

qa.q: Why might Siddharth have said 'Yep, doable' while leaving tasks untouched?
qa.a: In a room where only yes felt safe, he likely couldn't voice his disagreement, so it came out as quiet non-delivery.

qa.q: What change did Manoj make, and why did it work?
qa.a: Ending planning by asking what was a bad idea and then waiting, which made 'no' safe and let Siddharth raise the real risk. 🤔

qa.q: How might the colleague have seen Manoj's meetings?
qa.a: As a place where everyone nodded along, which is why the colleague asked whether anyone had ever said no.

grounding: A manager recalls a team member who agreed in every meeting and then delivered nothing, and how making it safe to say no changed things.

passage:
Uday had been saying "fine" all evening in their Hyderabad flat. Fine about dinner, fine about the weekend plan, fine about her mother visiting. He put the plates down a little too hard. He answered her messages with a single thumbs-up. Pallavi noticed the way he sighed when she mentioned Sunday.
She could have asked, "What's your problem?" Instead she sat on the arm of the sofa. "I think I might have missed something," she said. "You seem annoyed, and I'd really rather hear it straight than guess. I won't be upset if it's about me."
Uday looked at the TV for a while. Then: "You said yes to your mother's visit without asking me. It's the third weekend in a row."
Pallavi nodded. "That's fair. Let's plan the next one together."
His shoulders dropped. Later he even laughed at something on the TV.

qa.q: What did Uday answer Pallavi's messages with?
qa.a: A single thumbs-up.

qa.q: What does Uday putting the plates down too hard suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Irritated about something he hadn't said, with the annoyance leaking out through small actions.

qa.q: Which choice of Pallavi's made directness safe for Uday?
qa.a: Saying she might have missed something and would rather hear it straight, and promising not to be upset, instead of asking 'What's your problem?'

qa.q: What might Uday have felt after Pallavi said 'That's fair'?
qa.a: Relieved and heard; his dropped shoulders and later laugh show the tension no longer needed to leak out sideways.

grounding: A woman senses her husband's veiled irritation, says she may have missed something and welcomes a straight answer, and the tension eases.

passage:
I noticed it first in Jomon's emails: "Per my last email", "As previously mentioned", "Just circling back for the third time". Polite words with teeth. At stand-up he'd say, "Great, love that," in a voice that meant the opposite. I had been team lead for two months, and he had been passed over for the post.
I could have ignored it, or matched his tone. Instead, one afternoon I asked him to have tea with me in the canteen. I said, "Jomon, I think I might have missed something with you. If you're annoyed with me or with how things are running, I'd rather hear it straight. You won't get in trouble for it."
He looked surprised. Then he told me: I had changed his reporting format without asking. Small, but it stung, on top of the promotion. I changed it back. His emails got shorter after that. I'm Seema, and I still use that sentence.

qa.a: "Per my last email", "As previously mentioned" and "Just circling back for the third time".

qa.a: Stung that his reporting format was changed without asking, on top of being passed over, and unsure it was safe to say so.

qa.q: Which choice of Seema's made directness possible?
qa.a: Inviting Jomon for tea and saying Seema might have missed something, welcoming a straight answer with no trouble attached.

qa.q: What would have changed if Seema had matched Jomon's tone?
qa.a: The sniping would likely have grown, and Seema might never have learned about the reporting format or fixed it.

subtype: Different selves at school and home [Actor]
passage:
Jasleen, you think I'm loud? At school, sure. I'm the one who argues with the debate judge and does the Hindi teacher impression. But you've never seen me at home. At home I'm... tiny. I say "ji" to everything. I don't argue with Papa about anything, not even what I want to study. I eat quietly and go to my room. My parents think I'm shy. Mummy once told a relative, "Alka hardly talks." I laughed so hard inside.
It's easier, honestly. At home, loud gets me in trouble; at school, quiet gets me ignored. So I keep them apart. Never invite friends home, never let Mummy come to the debate finals. But sometimes it's lonely. Nobody at school knows I want to do fine arts. Nobody at home knows I won the debate trophy. Both halves of me are only half known.

qa.q: What did Mummy once tell a relative about Alka?
qa.a: "Alka hardly talks."

qa.q: Why does keeping school and home apart feel easier to Alka?

I'm Dolma, and Anirban sits next to me in Class 11. At school he's the loudest person in the room: captain of the quiz team, cracking jokes, arguing with the physics teacher about black holes.
Last Sunday I went to his flat to drop off lab notes. His grandfather opened the door, and Anirban appeared behind him, and he was a different person. He spoke in a small voice. He didn't make a single joke. When his grandfather asked who I was, Anirban said, "Just a classmate, Dadu," and took the notes at the door without asking me in.
On Monday he was loud again, as if Sunday hadn't happened. I don't know what it's like in his home. But I wonder how many people really know him, the school Anirban or the Sunday one.

qa.a: His grandfather.

qa.q: Why might Anirban have said 'Just a classmate, Dadu' and kept Dolma at the door?

qa.a: As a quiet, polite boy, probably with no idea he captains the quiz team and argues about black holes.

March. At school, Yusuf was the class clown and the first to volunteer for anything. At home he said almost nothing; his father liked a quiet house, and his older brothers did all the talking. When Abhinav asked to come over for a project, Yusuf said, "My house is under repair," which wasn't true.
June. Abhinav's mother offered to bring Yusuf's parents to the school play, where Yusuf had the lead. Yusuf panicked and told his parents it was cancelled. On the night he performed brilliantly, then scanned the crowd and felt oddly empty.
September. Yusuf's mother found the play programme in his bag. "You had the main role?" she said, stunned. "Why didn't you tell us?" Yusuf shrugged, then said quietly, "At home I'm a different person." She sat down. "I'd like to meet the other one too."

qa.q: What did Yusuf tell his parents about the school play?
qa.a: That it was cancelled.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf feel 'oddly empty' after performing brilliantly?
qa.a: His family wasn't there to see the confident side of him, because he had kept his two worlds sealed apart.

qa.q: What turning point in September could start joining Yusuf's two worlds?
qa.a: His mother finding the programme and saying she'd like to meet 'the other one too', which invites him to bring his school self home.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel after hearing the house was 'under repair'?
qa.a: Maybe a little shut out, sensing Yusuf keeps part of life closed, without knowing why.

grounding: Over several months a teenager who is bold at school and quiet at home keeps the worlds apart, until his mother discovers the other side.

Their hostel room, Tuesday night.
"Damini, you're studying? Your Mamaji's funeral was only yesterday."
"Exam's on Thursday, Siami. Organic chemistry."
"Do you want to talk about him?"
"Not now." Damini underlined a reaction. "I've put him in a box. Just till the exam's over."
"A box?"
"In my head. With a lid. Friday evening I open it."
"Is that... okay?"

Friday evening, same room.
"How was the exam?"
"Good. Really good, actually." Damini's voice wobbled. "Siami, can you sit with me? I'm opening the box now."
Lalremsiami closed her laptop and sat on the bed beside Damini, who cried for a long time, holding her Mamaji's last letter.

qa.q: Which exam did Damini have on Thursday?
qa.a: Organic chemistry.

qa.a: It let her focus on the exam he would have wanted her to pass, knowing she had set a time to grieve afterwards.

qa.q: What choice made the box helpful rather than harmful?
qa.a: Setting a clear time to open it, Friday evening after the exam, and asking Siami to sit with her while she grieved.

qa.a: Worried and unsure whether it was okay, which is why she asked; she was ready to support Damini when the box opened.

passage:
My Dadi died three days before my semester finals. I was nineteen. I remember the phone call, then deciding very calmly: not now. I'll feel this after the last paper. I studied twelve hours a day. I didn't cry at the prayer meeting; I sat at the back with my notes. My cousin Ritu thought I was cold. I wasn't. I had just packed everything into a trunk and sat on the lid.
I topped two papers. Then, on the evening after the last exam, I went to Dadi's room at home, opened her steel cupboard and smelled her talcum powder, and the trunk burst open. I cried for two days. Ritu brought me tea and her old photo album.
Looking back, I, Kalyani, think the trunk helped me get through. But it only worked because I actually opened it.

qa.q: When did Kalyani's Dadi die?
qa.a: Three days before the semester finals.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani decide so calmly, 'not now'?
qa.a: Kalyani wanted to get through the finals and felt grief would swamp the studying, so packing it away felt like the only way to cope for the moment.

qa.q: What made the 'trunk' a healthy pause and not an escape?
qa.a: Opening it after the last exam, going to Dadi's room and letting the grief come, with Ritu there with tea and photos.

qa.q: Why might Ritu have thought Kalyani was cold at the prayer meeting?
qa.a: Ritu saw no tears, only notes, and couldn't see that Kalyani had packed the grief away to open later.

grounding: A student whose grandmother died just before finals boxes up the grief to study, does well, and then lets it out after the last paper.

Warden's note, Girls' Hostel, 28 April
Vasudha's grandfather died on the 20th, during exam week. She went home for one day for the rites and came back the next evening. Since then she has studied late in the common room, eaten her meals and sat every paper. Her roommate says she hasn't talked about him at all.
She told me, "I'll grieve properly after the 30th. I can't fall apart now." I respect that; setting grief aside for a short while can be a way to cope. But I don't want the box to stay shut for good.
Next step: I've spoken to her. We agreed she'll go home for three days after the last paper, and I've given her the counsellor's number in case the feelings come sooner. I'll check in with her on 1 May.
Parul Sharma, Warden

qa.a: On the 20th, during exam week.

passage:
The first time I visited Kamal's clinic, I watched him with a crying child: kneeling, voice soft, making up a story about a brave elephant. Three patients later he was still smiling. I was so proud.
Then he came home at nine and I asked about his day, and he said, "Fine." I asked if he wanted dal or khichdi, and he said, "Whatever. Doesn't matter." He scrolled on his phone through dinner. For months I thought he had simply stopped caring about me.
One night I said so, gently. He put the phone down and looked stricken. "I use it all up," he said. "By the time I get home there's nothing left."
We agreed on a small thing: twenty minutes alone on the balcony when he gets in, then real time together. Some nights I, Arohi, get the soft voice now too.

qa.q: What story did Kamal make up for the crying child?
qa.a: A story about a brave elephant.

qa.q: Why did Arohi start to believe Kamal had stopped caring?
qa.a: His warmth went to patients while at home he gave one-word answers and scrolled his phone, so Arohi felt left with only the tired leftovers.

qa.q: What choice did the couple make, and why does it help?
qa.a: Twenty minutes alone on the balcony for Kamal when he gets home, so he can recharge before real time together.

qa.q: What does Kamal's line 'I use it all up' suggest about his side of it?
qa.a: He isn't cold on purpose; his patience goes into patients all day, and he is drained by the time he reaches home.

grounding: A spouse notices that their partner is patient and charming with patients but curt at home, and learns his energy is spent before he gets there.

What I've noticed about Francis over the last month:
- At work events he is warm, funny and patient. His customers at the bank adore him. Last Friday I watched him listen to an old man's complaint for twenty minutes without once checking his watch.

Tuesday
Went to pick Manjula up from school today and watched from the gate. Forty Class 2 kids around her, and she was laughing, crouching to tie laces, praising a wobbly drawing as if it were a masterpiece. A parent stopped me: "Your wife is a saint." I agreed.
At home she dropped her bag, said, "Please don't talk to me for a bit," and lay on the sofa with her eyes shut. When I asked what she wanted for dinner, she said, "I don't care, Devika, anything." It stung. It always stings.
But I've started to see it: she isn't cold to me. She's spent. Every drop of patience goes to those forty kids. I get the empty cup.
Tomorrow I'll ask her: can we have Sunday mornings where nobody needs anything from her, and then a proper walk, just us? I miss the laughing version.
Devika

qa.a: "Your wife is a saint."

qa.a: Sunday mornings with nothing asked of Manjula, then a walk together, giving her time to refill before their time as a couple. 🤍

qa.a: Constantly giving patience and warmth to forty children, which leaves her exhausted by the time she gets home.

passage:
Last year I had two sealed rooms. In one was my education loan: three missed payments and a letter from the bank I kept in a drawer. In the other was my relationship, slowly ending over video calls. At work I was bright and efficient; nobody knew about either. With my boyfriend I never mentioned money. With my parents I never mentioned him. It worked, sort of. I kept functioning.
Then one Tuesday the bank called during a client meeting, and that same evening he said he wanted to break up. Both doors burst open at once. I sat in the office washroom and couldn't stop shaking. My friend Nazia found me there. I told her everything, the loan and the breakup, the first time I'd said both out loud. She didn't fix anything. She helped me write a list of who to call the next morning. I'm Shreya, and I keep fewer sealed rooms now.

qa.q: What did Shreya keep in a drawer?
qa.a: A letter from the bank.

qa.q: Why did keeping the two problems sealed apart work for Shreya, at least for a while?
qa.a: Separating them let Shreya stay bright and efficient at work and avoid facing both worries at once.

qa.q: What turning point helped Shreya begin to deal with both problems?
qa.a: Telling Nazia everything in the washroom and making a list of who to call the next morning, instead of sealing the doors again.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Nazia to find Shreya in the washroom?
qa.a: Probably alarming, since Shreya always seemed so capable, and moving to hear how much had been hidden.

grounding: An adult keeps a loan problem and a failing relationship in separate sealed compartments until both burst open on the same day.

Supervisor's note, 9 October
Sumit has been one of our steadiest engineers this year: calm in a crisis, never brings personal matters to work. Today that changed. During the client call he froze mid-sentence, excused himself, and I found him sitting in the stairwell with his head in his hands.
He told me, reluctantly, that his father's shop has been in debt for months and he has been sending money home, and that his marriage is strained because he hasn't told his wife. He said he kept work, money and home in "separate boxes" so he could keep functioning. This morning his wife found the bank messages and they argued; then the client call started.
Next steps: I gave him the rest of the day off. I pointed him to our confidential employee counselling line. We'll meet on Monday about his workload.
Urmila

qa.a: Sitting in the stairwell with his head in his hands.

qa.a: It let him keep functioning at work while carrying the debt and the strain at home, without facing everything at once.

qa.q: Which of Urmila's steps is most useful, and why?
qa.a: Pointing him to the confidential counselling line, because he needs somewhere to open the boxes with support, not just a day off.

qa.q: How might Sumit's wife have felt finding the bank messages?
qa.a: Shocked and hurt at being shut out of something so big, which is why they argued.

Tried to count today how many things I don't say to whom. At work: nothing about Damini and me arguing every night about whether to move to Pune. With Damini: nothing about the credit-card balance I've been rolling over since Diwali. With Ammi: nothing about either. I've built a flat with every door locked. Tomorrow I'll tell Damini about the card. Just one door. One at a time.
Tanvir
